sources.text: TREJOLab Cell signaling in health and disease About Us OUR WORK WELCOME! Our research is focused on understanding the cell signaling pathways that control vascular inflammation and breast cancer progression. We are a team of outstanding science scholars including students, postdoctoral fellows, and research staff associates. The TREJOLab is located in the School of Medicine on the UC San Diego Health Sciences campus in La Jolla, CA. Contact Us: JoAnn Trejo, Ph.D Principal Investigator Tel: 858-246-0150 Email: joanntrejo@ucsd.edu TREJOLab Contact Carolyne Bardeleben, PhD SRA4, Lab Manager Tel: 858-246-0343 Email: cbardeleben@health.ucsd.edu Office of Faculty Affairs Contact Virginia Hazen, Ph.D. Email: hsfacaffairs@ucsd.edu Tel: 619-543-3274 Trejo Lab School of Medicine, MC 0636 Biomedical Sciences Building, Rooms 3041, 3045, 3044 Tel: 858-246-0343

JoAnn Trejo, Ph.D. Professor of Pharmacology Senior Assistant Vice Chancellor for Health Sciences Faculty Affairs
sources.text: JoAnn Trejo, Ph.D. Professor of Pharmacology Senior Assistant Vice Chancellor for Health Sciences Faculty Affairs FACULTY PROFILE STYLESHEET: do not remove this block JoAnn Trejo, Ph.D. Professor of Pharmacology Senior Assistant Vice Chancellor for Health Sciences Faculty Affairs Research Interests Our research is focused on cell signaling and how it controls vascular inflammation and cancer. We study the function of G protein-coupled receptors, specifically protease-activated receptors, the tumor suppressor alpha-arrestin ARRDC3 and ubiquitin-driven inflammatory signaling. We discovered that ubiquitination of a subset of GPCRs initiates p38 inflammatory signaling and endothelial dysfunction. A major challenge is to understand how this pathway is regulated. We also discovered a new GPCR lysosomal sorting pathway that is regulated by the adaptor proteins ALIX and alpha-arrestin ARRDC3 – this pathway is dysregulated in invasive cancer. Another challenge is to understand how and why GPCRs sort into the ALIX and ARRDC3- dependent lysosomal sorting pathway and the impact of the tumor suppressor ARRDC3 on GPCR signaling and cancer progression.
